content: SDHC stands for succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit C. This term can refer to either the protein subunit itself or the gene that encodes this protein. The succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) protein complex is an enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate, with the simultaneous reduction of ubiquinone to ubiquinol. Specifically, the reaction can be summarized as: succinate + ubiquinone → fumarate + ubiquinol. The SDHA subunit of the SDH complex is connected to the SDHB subunit at the hydrophilic, catalytic end of the complex. Electrons removed from succinate are transferred from SDHA to SDHB and then to the SDHC and SDHD subunits, which are located at the hydrophobic end of the complex embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. Function of the SDHC Protein The SDH complex is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane and plays a dual role in cellular metabolism, participating in both the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) and the respiratory chain. SDHC functions as an intermediary in the enzymatic activity of the SDH complex: The SDHA subunit converts succinate to fumarate as part of the citric acid cycle. This reaction also converts FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) to FADH2. Electrons from FADH2 are transferred to the iron-sulfur clusters of the SDHB subunit. This step is part of the respiratory chain. Finally, the electrons are transferred to the ubiquinone (Q) pool via the SDHC and SDHD subunits. Gene Encoding SDHC The gene that encodes the SDHC protein is nuclear, even though the protein itself is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. In humans, the SDHC gene is located on chromosome 1 at position q21. It is composed of six exons and encodes a protein consisting of 170 amino acids. Historically, SDHC was also referred to as PGL3.
